title: Five remembrances
hookLine: the Buddha's five: I will age, fall ill, die, be parted from what I love, and my actions are my own (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57)

cards: Here's a list nobody pins to the fridge. Not the dentist appointment, but the big ones underneath: getting old, getting sick, the people you'll one day lose. That list usually stays folded.
Yet one teacher asked people, women and men, householders and monks alike, to take it out and read it. Often. Slowly.

Not to frighten themselves, but because, he said, it loosens something. This week has kept endings in view: the view from above, memento mori, Seneca's rehearsal, the hug that counts. The Buddha closes it with his list.

teach.b: It comes from a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of the Buddha's numbered discourses, book of fives, number fifty-seven. In plain words: One: I will grow old; I can't escape aging.
Two: I will fall ill; I can't escape illness. Three: I will die; I can't escape death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them.
Five: my actions are my own. I am their owner and their heir; whatever I do, good or harmful, that is what I will inherit. The surprise is who it's for.
The text says women and men, householders and monks, should reflect on these often. Not just the monastery. Everyone.
And it gives reasons. Remembering age softens the pride of youth. Illness, the pride of health.
Death, the pride of simply being alive. Remembering parting loosens the grip of craving. Then the fifth turns everything around.
The first four are about what will happen to you. The fifth is about what you do.
Age, illness, death and parting are not up to you.
That may echo the line Epictetus drew earlier this month, though the two come from different worlds and mean different things.
In the Buddha's list, the one thing you truly own is your conduct.
So the list doesn't end in gloom. It ends in your hands. You can't stop the clock.
You can choose what you say at dinner tonight.

how: In some Buddhist communities, including Theravada monasteries and Plum Village practice centers, the five remembrances are recited aloud as part of a chanting session.

the list ends on what you do, not what happens to you
the fifth: my actions are my own; I am their owner and their heir.

games.q: you've just read four remembrances: age, illness, death, parting. what does the fifth one say?
o: so enjoy it while it lasts.
games.why: the fifth turns the list around: I am the owner and heir of my actions. the first four aren't up to you; this one is.

practice: Say each one inside, with a whole breath before the next: I will grow old; I will fall ill; I will die; I will be parted from what I love; my actions are my own. If one of them stings, let it, and soften the shoulders.
Then stay with the fifth, and let it point at one thing you'll do today.

wordCard.voice: Five remembrances. Four things that will happen to everyone, and one thing that belongs to you: what you do. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, kammassako: owner of one's actions, from kamma (action). the word inside the fifth remembrance.

carryVoice: Your line: my actions are my own. Four things happen to you; the fifth is yours. Tomorrow: up, and walking.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.57 (Upajjhatthana Sutta, subjects for frequent reflection)
